clue.text: Weed that succeeded like Lawrence in conflict

parts.note: something that succeeded has passed, as in an exam

indicators.note: in tells us one piece sits inside the other, Lawrence within the conflict

parts.note: war is armed conflict
T.E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia, goes by his initials TE

explanation.surface: A plant that thrived, like Lawrence of Arabia during the war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weed' looks like a plant but is read as wee'd, the past tense of urinating; 'like' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To wee is to urinate, so having wee'd is a jokey spelling of having urinated.

clue.text: Like the proposal to ban hunting?

definitions.text: Like the proposal to ban hunting?

parts.words: Like the proposal to ban hunting?
parts.note: the parliamentary bill to ban fox hunting seemed to be debated endlessly, a proposal that never went away

explanation.surface: A remark on the never-ending debate over banning fox hunting in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: A proposal in a debate is a motion; the hunting ban came back to Parliament so often it seemed endless. The phrase usually means a machine that runs forever.
explanation.definitionFit: A proposal debated forever is a never-ending motion, punning on the impossible machine that never stops.

clue.text: Heartless colleens rejected love in Ireland

indicators.note: rejected means the remaining letters are sent back, read in reverse
heartless means the middle letter of the word is taken away

parts.note: colleen is an Irish word for a girl
love is zero in tennis scoring, the letter O

explanation.surface: Unfeeling Irish girls spurned love somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' drops R, the centre of GIRLS, leaving GILS; 'rejected' turns that to SLIG. 'Ireland' defines a place in it: Sligo is a county and town in the west of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Sligo is a county and town in Ireland, so it is a place found in Ireland.

clue.text: English trees are rubbish

parts.note: the yew is a tree
the ash is a tree

explanation.surface: A claim that English trees are no good.
explanation.walkthrough: The one word 'trees' supplies two different trees in a row; 'are' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyewash is informal for nonsense, talk meant to deceive, so it means rubbish.

clue.text: Straw's negotiation with the Spanish is profligate

indicators.note: negotiation suggests the word is worked over and its letters reshaped

parts.note: Straw (Jack Straw, the British politician) gives its letters to be rearranged
el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Jack Straw's dealings with Spain are wasteful.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Straw was British Foreign Secretary, so negotiating with the Spanish fits the surface; 'negotiation' rearranges STRAW into WASTR.
explanation.definitionFit: A wastrel is a spendthrift, someone profligate with money; here the noun stands for a profligate person.

clue.text: To have wine's no good for drinking health

parts.note: Asti is an Italian sparkling wine

explanation.surface: Drinking wine is said to be no good for your health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drinking health' means drinking to someone's health; 'have' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Toasting is raising a glass and drinking to someone's good health.

clue.text: 20's turnover

parts.note: 20 is the grower of crops; his turnover is the yearly changing of what each field grows

explanation.surface: A remark on a business's turnover.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 is the answer to 20-down; turnover means business income on the surface, but here it means turning over which crop goes in which field.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotation of crops is the farming practice of changing a field's crop each season, a turning over.

clue.text: Composer about to offer a lift?

parts.note: C is short for circa, about
hop in is what a driver says offering someone a lift

explanation.surface: A composer about to give someone a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'about to' as 'on the point of'; split it so 'about' is C.
explanation.definitionFit: Chopin was a Polish Romantic composer and pianist.

clue.text: Cactus not spoken of lightly

annotationWithheld.why: Cactus not spoken of lightly (6): CEREUS sounds like SERIOUS, but SERIOUS is 'not ... lightly' wrapped round 'spoken of', the homophone signal, so 'spoken' does two jobs and no contiguous leaf gives the word said aloud

clue.text: One drug after another for leading lady

indicators.note: after places the second drug behind the first

parts.note: heroin is a drug
another drug: E is short for ecstasy

explanation.surface: A tale of one drug following another, about an actress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One drug after another' reads as a drug binge; 'another' means another drug, ecstasy.
explanation.definitionFit: A heroine is the female lead of a story or film, the leading lady.

clue.text: Bobby has a foot in footwear

indicators.note: in places the article and the abbreviation inside the footwear

parts.note: a shoe is footwear

explanation.surface: Someone named Bobby with a foot in a shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: Bobby Shafto(e) is the hero of an English folk song who went to sea with silver buckles on his knee; 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Bobby Shaftoe is the sailor of the traditional English nursery song, so the first name points to the surname.

clue.text: A right posture perhaps, but it couldn't procure its posterity

indicators.note: perhaps suggests these letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A good posture, perhaps, but one that failed to secure the future.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges A, R and POSTURE; 'but' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The pterosaur, a flying reptile, died out, so it failed to leave descendants: it could not secure posterity.

clue.text: Some get it less from desert than cunning

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some people earn less from merit than from guile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desert' is what one deserves, not sand; the definition is a cryptic one about honours earned by merit rather than craft.
explanation.definitionFit: A title, an honour like a knighthood, is ideally earned by merit, what one deserves, rather than by cunning.

clue.text: In Europe we find common sense

definitions.meaning: French for we, French being a European language
British informal for practical good sense

explanation.surface: Somewhere in Europe we find good sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'find' is a link between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the French first-person plural pronoun, and in British slang it means practical intelligence.

clue.text: Monk spoken of in London as criminal

indicators.note: Cockney London speech swaps TH and F sounds, so a word said in London may come out changed

parts.note: felonious means criminal

explanation.surface: A monk said in London to be a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: Monk is the jazz pianist Thelonious Monk, not a friar; a Cockney (Londoner) famously confuses TH and F, so 'felonious' and the first name sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Thelonious is the first name of jazz pianist Monk, so the surname leads to the given name.

clue.text: "Plantagenets" given wrongly in response

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the abbreviation for response

parts.note: ANS is short for answer, a response

indicators.note: wrongly means the letters of the word are set down out of order

explanation.surface: Someone answers 'Plantagenets' incorrectly in a quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' rearranges the clue's own word into GEVIN, which 'in' places inside the abbreviation. The quotation marks show the dynasty's name is being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: The Plantagenet kings descended from the counts of Anjou, so they are also called Angevins.

clue.text: Friend in German capital city such as 17

parts.note: a pal is a friend
D is the abbreviation for German (Deutsch)
Rome is the capital city of Italy

explanation.surface: A friend in a German capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 is 17-down, ROTATOR, which reads the same backwards. The surface suggests Berlin, but the capital is Rome and 'German' is just D.
explanation.definitionFit: A palindrome reads the same both ways, and 17's answer is one example of the kind.

clue.text: Source of Hamlet?

parts.note: read hamlet as a little ham; the young animal that grows into pork is its source

explanation.surface: A question about where Shakespeare got Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for Shakespeare's source; '-let' means small, so a hamlet is jokily a little ham, and a young pig is where ham comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A young pig is the origin of ham, so it is jokingly the source of a small ham.

clue.text: Turner's rubbish? Yes, possibly

parts.note: a device that turns is a turner; it opens with a word for rubbish, and the whole word reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a painting by J.M.W. Turner is rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner the painter is the misdirection: a turner is anything that turns. ROT (rubbish) starts it and, as 16-across says, the word is a palindrome, ending with ROT backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotator is a thing that rotates, a turner; it begins with a synonym of rubbish.

clue.text: M is follicularly unchallenged

parts.note: the letter M is the head, the first letter, of the word mop; a person with thick hair has a head like a mop

explanation.surface: A statement that someone called M has plenty of hair.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the head of MOP; 'follicularly unchallenged' is a jokey way of saying not bald.
explanation.definitionFit: A mophead is a person with a thick shock of hair, the opposite of bald.

clue.text: Stock support

parts.note: stock means livestock, farm animals; what they stand on supports them

explanation.surface: Backing for the stock market.
explanation.walkthrough: Stock reads as shares; it is livestock, which stand on their feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoof is the horny foot of cattle, horses and other livestock, which supports them.

clue.text: There's little doubt one's cultivated

parts.note: one's cultivated means one who has cultivated land; a short hesitation, er, ends the word and land worked for crops begins it

explanation.surface: A claim that someone is plainly refined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cultivated' reads as refined but means having tilled fields; 'one's' is one has. The word is FARM plus ER, the sound of a little doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmer is a person who cultivates land, so he is one who has cultivated.

clue.text: Assault on a G-string?

parts.note: rope is a kind of thick string

explanation.surface: An attack on a skimpy piece of underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: A G-string is skimpy underwear; read it as G plus string, ROPE. 'on a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To grope someone is to touch them sexually without consent, a form of assault.

clue.text: Performer, a desperate character surrounded by tatty carpet

indicators.note: surrounded by puts the character inside the jumbled carpet
tatty means shabby and worn, so the letters of carpet are messed up

parts.note: Desperate Dan is a character from the British comic The Dandy

explanation.surface: An entertainer, a wild man, wrapped in a shabby rug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tatty' rearranges the floor covering into TAPCER, split around the comic hero; 'a' is a link. Desperate Dan is a strongman from the British children's comic The Dandy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tap dancer is a performer who dances in shoes with metal plates.

clue.text: Stoker has article written before one of the patriarchs

indicators.note: written before puts the article in front of the name

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
Bram Stoker wrote Dracula

explanation.surface: Dracula's author has a piece written ahead of a biblical figure.
explanation.walkthrough: A stoker shovels coal, but this is Bram Stoker; 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Abram is the original name of Abraham, first of the Hebrew patriarchs in Genesis.

clue.text: 12 is unusually select

indicators.note: unusually says the letters are put in an uncommon order

parts.note: 12 refers to 12-across, whose answer is used here
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rank that is unusually exclusive.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 is 12-across, TITLE; 'unusually' rearranges it with IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Elitist means favouring an exclusive few, so it describes something select.

clue.text: Feature of man with 12 and gong

parts.note: 12 is 12-across, a rank; an earl holds one such rank
gong is British slang for a medal or honour, such as the OBE

explanation.surface: A man with a title and a medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 is 12-across, TITLE, and an earl is one example; OBE is the Order of the British Empire, an honour. 'with' and 'and' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: The earlobe is a part of the human ear, a feature of a man.

clue.text: Fortune-teller's back on the fiddle, giving some amusement

indicators.note: back says the little word is read the other way round

parts.note: a Strad is a Stradivarius violin, the fiddle par excellence

indicators.note: some takes only part of the word that follows, its opening letters

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller is back to cheating, which is quite amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the fiddle' reads as cheating; 'back' turns ON into NO, and 'some' takes AMUS from 'amusement'. 's and 'giving' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Nostradamus was a sixteenth-century French seer famous for his prophecies.
